properties.name: ROOT CAUSE (walked, measured): a second --http server started on a store another process holds does NOT exit. It serves the one-tool degraded surface, stays up and listening, and never retries the open: measured still degraded 11 s after the first server stopped. So a rolling update's new pod looks alive, the old pod is removed, and the design stays unavailable until someone restarts the pod. A TRANSIENT cause (a held lock) is treated like a permanent one. Second member of the "a stand-in surface never re-probes" class
properties.statement:
RUN AS THE SKILL (root-cause, fetched fresh), 2026-09-28, triaging art:github-issue-616-oauth-resource-server (Alex, GitHub issue #616, 2026-09-28, reflow2 0.70.0) under rule:field-feedback-issues-are-root-caused-and-ideas-are-brainstormed. Measured on 0.74.0.

① OBSERVED, the reporter's words: "A StatefulSet, not a Deployment: a rolling update briefly runs two pods and the second can't take the lock." EXPECTED: either the second instance fails in a way the orchestrator sees and retries, or it waits for the lock and then serves the design. NOT AFFECTED: a single instance, and --shared locally, whose client respawns a dead daemon.

② PRECEDENT (search_design on the lock text and "degraded … never retries"): cap:degraded-surface and req:never-silently-absent make a failed open speak in band. fact:root-cause-the-opt-in-was-finished-by-a-client-command-and-the-latent-process-never-grew-the-surface (2026-09-14) is the same shape one surface over: the latent process "never re-probed or grew the surface", and the in-place promotion an August report asked for was never built.

③ CANDIDATES.
(A) The second server exits with an error and the orchestrator restarts it, so this is only a documentation note.
(B) It serves degraded and recovers by itself once the lock frees.
(C) It serves degraded, stays up, and never retries.
(D) THE OBSERVATION IS WRONG: the lock is not the problem, only the volume's single attachment.

④ WHAT SEPARATES THEM: whether the process exits, and the second server's tool list before and after the first stops.

⑤ RESULTS (scratch store; server A `--http 127.0.0.1:0`; then server B on the same --graph-path):
· B did not exit. It ran until its 12 s timeout (exit 124), logged "another process already has the design graph at … open. The graph is single-writer … Stop that server … and run this again", then "serving the DEGRADED surface over HTTP at … Fix the cause above and restart to serve it properly", and listened on its port. ⇒ A REFUTED.
· B's tools/list while A held the lock: 1 tool (reflow2_unavailable). A was stopped with SIGTERM, then B's tools/list at +3 s: 1, and at +11 s: 1. B's stderr has no retry or reopen line. ⇒ B REFUTED, C HOLDS.
· D is not separable here. On a cluster a ReadWriteOnce volume may also refuse the second attachment, but when both pods land on one node the lock is what refuses, and that is the case measured.

⑥ CLASS: a stand-in surface (degraded, or latent) is a terminal state even when its cause is transient. A held lock clears on its own, a missing design can be created, and neither process ever re-probes. The fix at the class is to retry, or to exit non-zero, for causes that can clear. It would also have answered the 2026-09-14 latent-surface report, which rewording the instruction alone did not. Serving the reason in band (req:never-silently-absent) stays right either way; what is wrong is also looking healthy forever.

⑦ OUT OF SCOPE (no code changed). A test pinning the class: server B started on a store server A holds serves the degraded surface; after A stops, B serves the design within a stated bound, or B exits non-zero promptly, whichever is chosen. And the reason stays in band until then. Deciding between "retry in place" and "exit so the orchestrator restarts" is a real choice: exiting breaks the one-tool explanation for a stdio client, and retrying needs a bound.

REPORTER'S CONCLUSIONS: HELD that the second instance cannot take the lock. The advice (one replica, a StatefulSet) is sound. The measurement adds that the failure is not a crash an orchestrator would notice: it looks healthy and does not recover.

⑨ NOT ESTABLISHED: what Alex's cluster actually did (pods, probes, volume access mode); whether --serve-shared behaves differently from --http here (not measured; its client-side respawn is a different path).

ADDED THE SAME DAY, from the image itself: the published image's HEALTHCHECK is a bare TCP connect, `bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/8080'` (Dockerfile:143-144). A degraded server binds its port, so the image's own health check reports it HEALTHY. That holds for this held-lock case and for the sidecar-less refusal (fact:root-cause-the-registry-drops-a-store-without-identity-and-says-no-designs-2026-09-28). The one signal an orchestrator reads by default is the one that cannot tell a served design from a degraded one.
